procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 21.01.2019 of High Court for the State of Telangana at Hyderabad in CRLP No. 3988 of 2016, CRLP No. 11942 of 2018 and WP No. 2253 of 2018
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the cognizance taken by the Special Court and prayed for quashing the complaints, arguing that they were public servants and prior sanction under Section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was required. issue.issue_text: At what stage of the proceedings can the question of sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure be raised?

facts: The case involved complaints filed under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, against public servants.

The High Court had quashed the trial court's order taking cognizance of the complaints, ruling that prior sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) was necessary at the outset.
law: Section 197 of the CrPC states that no court shall take cognizance of an offence alleged to have been committed by a public servant while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, except with the previous sanction of the government.
application: The Supreme Court established that the question of sanction under Section 197 is not a preliminary issue that must be decided only before or at the time of taking cognizance.

The Court clarified that this issue can be raised at any point in the proceedings after cognizance has been taken. This includes immediately after cognizance, at the stage of framing charges, during the trial, or even at the conclusion of the trial.
The Court reasoned that in some cases, it is not possible to determine if the alleged act was committed in the discharge of official duty without evidence being presented.

To decide whether the public servant's claim (that the act was part of their official duty) is reasonable and not a mere pretense, the court may need to give the defense an opportunity to present evidence during the trial.
Therefore, in such situations, the court can leave the question of sanction open and decide it as part of the final judgment after the trial is complete.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the question of sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC can be raised at any stage of the proceedings after cognizance is taken, and its determination can be deferred until the conclusion of the trial if evidence is needed to decide the issue.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of the question of sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be deferred until the conclusion of the trial?

law.fact_text: Under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a public servant cannot be prosecuted for an offense alleged to have been committed while acting in the discharge of official duty without prior sanction from the government.
law.relevant_text: 197. Prosecution of Judges and public servants.— (1) When any person who is or was a Judge or Magistrate or a public servant not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government, is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty, no Court shall take cognizance of such offence except with the previous sanction

law.fact_text: The question of whether sanction is required can be raised at any stage of the legal proceedings, from after the court takes cognizance of the offense to the conclusion of the trial.
law.relevant_text: It is well settled that question of sanction under Section 197 of the Code can be raised any time after the cognizance; maybe immediately after cognizance or framing of charge or even at the time of conclusion of trial and after conviction as well.

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that in certain cases, it is not possible to effectively decide the question of sanction at a preliminary stage.
application.relevant_text: But there may be certain cases where it may not be possible to decide the question effectively without giving opportunity to the defence to establish that what he did was in discharge of official duty.

application.fact_text: A trial is necessary to give the accused an opportunity to present evidence and establish that their actions were reasonably connected to their official duties.
application.relevant_text: In order to come to the conclusion whether claim of the accused that the act that he did was in course of the performance of his duty was a reasonable one and neither pretended nor fanciful, can be examined during the course of trial by giving opportunity to the defence to establish it.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the question of sanction under Section 197 can be deferred until the conclusion of the trial. This is particularly appropriate in cases where evidence, which can only be presented during the trial, is needed to determine whether the accused's actions were performed in the discharge of their official duty. In such situations, the issue should be left open and decided in the final judgment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The question of sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a jurisdictional bar that must be decided at the outset of proceedings, not deferred to trial. In this case, the acts alleged against the respondents—allocating water and allotting land—were found to have been committed while purporting to act in the discharge of their official duties, as there was a direct connection between the acts and the duties entrusted to them, thereby necessitating prior sanction for the court to take cognizance.
legal_tests_applied: The legislative mandate in sub-section (1) of Section 197 debarring a court from taking cognizance of an offence except with the previous sanction of the Government concerned touches the jurisdiction of the court.

To determine the applicability of Section 197(1), the court must assess whether the acts complained of are alleged to have been committed by a public servant in discharge of his official duty or purporting to be in the discharge of his official duty.
The court must examine if there is a connection between the public servant's duties and the acts complained of.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the issue of sanction should be decided at the time of trial was rejected because the requirement of sanction under Section 197 is a jurisdictional bar on the court's power to take cognizance.

The court disagreed with the appellant's submission that the respondents' acts were not done in the discharge of their official duties. Upon perusing the complaint, the court found that the alleged acts of allocating water and allotting land were directly related to the discharge of the duties entrusted to the respondents.
why_respondent_won: The court found that the acts alleged against the respondents were committed by them while purporting to act in the discharge of their official duties.

The court concluded that there was a clear connection between the respondents' duties and the acts complained of (allocation of water and allotment of land), which satisfied the conditions for the applicability of Section 197(1).
policy_considerations: The object of Section 197 is to protect public servants from prosecutions and to ensure that they are not prosecuted for anything they do in the discharge of their duties.
This provision is for the protection of honest and sincere officers, though the protection is not unqualified and they can be prosecuted with a previous sanction from the appropriate government.
